ADDRESS TO HIS MAJESTY THE KING
speechtext: I think it does. It will be up to us if we take to ourselves the right to amend the constitution in this country.

subsubtopic: ADDRESS TO HIS MAJESTY THE KING
speechtext: Will the Prime Minister agree with that?

subsubtopic: ADDRESS TO HIS MAJESTY THE KING
speechtext:
I don't know, but I am selling him ideas, and I hope he accepts them. Then again, there is a matter of a national labour code. Many of the members in this house who were here during the war went through the strikes after the war, and watched the industrial relations committee in action. Those members will also remember our attempts to hammer out a national labour code in this country, something that is absolutely necessary in order to secure uniformity of labour legislation across the country. Every time a member started to talk about a national code, one of our legal friends started waving the British North America Act. We were told we could not do that because section so-and-so of the British North America Act prohibits it. We were told we had to go over to the old country to get it amended. All right, now is the time to change it.
There is a national labour code, so-called, in existence. It is not a national labour code at all because it only embraces a very few industries that fall within the jurisdiction of the federal government. It is still not national. I want this parliament to have the right to change the constitution to enable us to establish a national labour code in this country which will empower the government to fix minimum wages and vacations with pay. No restrictions would be placed on the provinces if they wanted to raise those mini-mums. I believe, however, there should be a national minimum wage rate applicable all across Canada.
I should like to ask my friends from Quebec this question, and through them Mr. Duplessis, who so strongly guards the rights of the provinces. How much did he respect the rights of his municipalities in events which occurred not so long ago?

subsubtopic: ADDRESS TO HIS MAJESTY THE KING
ADDRESS TO HIS MAJESTY THE KING
speechtext:
I remember when the asbestos workers, who were working for very low wages and who were in a union known as the Catholic Syndicate-which could not be con-


sidered radical or communistic by any stretch of the imagination-used every piece of machinery Duplessis made available in order to settle the dispute. In the final analysis they were forced to take a stand to settle that dispute. Did Mr. Duplessis respect the rights of the municipalities when he sent in his police to smash the strike without any solicitation from the municipalities? He invaded their rights, smashed things up, and was not very particular at that time about democracy or conferences with the municipalities before he usurped their privileges.
I am afraid that Mr. Duplessis and those who oppose the steps now being taken by the federal government merely wish to retain a veto. It is not a matter of sitting down and reasoning out some methods for changing our constitution; it is a matter of retaining the machinery so that one province in this country can veto anything that means progress and advancement for the people.

ADDRESS TO HIS MAJESTY THE KING
speechtext: You know quite well it could not be that province.

subsubtopic: ADDRESS TO HIS MAJESTY THE KING
speechtext:
I do not know, but I will let you know after I hear my hon. friends on my left speak.
I just wish to say this, Mr. Speaker, that in these matters we cannot continue to think in terms of the past. So far as I am concerned, I believe we have reached the end of an age. We have closed the old book and are starting to write a new one. Society is developing new mechanics. I should like to remind those who argue that we should continue to go to the parliament of the United Kingdom for amendments to our constitution, and to retain the privy council as the final court of appeal, that the country to which we are still clinging on that basis has gone through a revolution and is going through a revolution. Canada today has to begin thinking in terms of the future and close the book on the past. The past offers us no guide for what is going to take place in the future in this world.
Great Britain no longer represents what it represented in 1867. Drastic changes have been made and will continue to be made in that country. It is time Canadians began to think for themselves in terms of building a nation and working out our own destiny in this world. There is no going back. We will either have to go forward or become stagnant and fall into disrepute in the eyes of the world. When I pick up a newspaper and see that the Canadian delegates at the United Nations are not in a position to vote on a

certain question because the federal government has not authority to legislate on that matter, I feel it must be very embarrassing to those delegates.
Now, Mr. Speaker, my time has nearly expired but I should like to leave this thought with the members of the house. So far as this group is concerned, it is not a matter of politics. On many occasions, we are accused of supporting the government. It is immaterial to us who proposes the legislation. If our group believes it is a step in the right direction, we will support the proposal. The measure may not go as far as we want to go, but if it is a step in the right direction, no matter who proposes it, we will support it. I believe the step the Prime Minister is now taking is a step that should have been taken back in 1935. It is unfinished business since that time. I complimented the Prime Minister on his courage in bringing this measure forward at this time so early in this session. The members who are debating the question will be able to carefully scrutinize what changes may be made.
In 1935 the dominion-provincial conference recommended this change. It is unfinished business since that time. I do not believe either Quebec or Nova Scotia, or any of the provinces who are sceptical about it, have anything to fear. I have been looking over the members of this house for the past month and I believe they compare favourably with the members of any house since I had the privilege of coming to Ottawa. Most of them are young and vocal. They have no inferiority complex; they are prepared to debate issues and have been debating them. I believe that with the sort of parliament we have now we should have no fear of accepting the responsibility of regulating the future of this country.

subsubtopic: ADDRESS TO HIS MAJESTY THE KING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure we have all listened with much pleasure to the address by the hon. member who has just taken his seat. He takes part in a good many of the debates in this house and always adds something to them. At the outset of his remarks, I was interested in hearing him take the Prime Minister on what might be termed a Cook's tour up the side of a high mountain and leave him at the top of that mountain. I might point out, Mr. Speaker, that the top of a mountain is a rather cold and slippery place, and even with the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) as his guide I am sure the Prime Minister would have to watch his step.
The hon. member also spoke about the humiliation which certain of our representatives feel when they attend the United Nations conventions because of their inability to carry
British North America Act out certain ideas which are within the jurisdiction of the provinces. It is that very thing, Mr. Speaker, to which the provinces are objecting. The hon. member seemed to indicate that he was willing for the provinces to lose some jurisdiction they now have, without being consulted as to why it should be taken from them. In closing his remarks, the hon. member also said that we are no longer going to Great Britain to have our constitution amended. During the course of this debate I have not heard one speaker advocate going to Great Britain to have our constitution amended. I am sure there is no member in this party who has advocated that our constitution should not be amended by the representatives of our own people. But what we are asking is that the whole constitution be amended at the one time. What we object to is its being amended piecemeal, as the resolution of the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) would suggest. Unless it is amended as has been suggested by our leader I am satisfied that, as he has clearly pointed out, we shall have to do the very thing that the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) objects to.
It is not my intention to prolong this debate to any great extent; but coming as I do from New Brunswick, which was one of the pillars of confederation, I felt that I should say a few words in this debate, particularly as no one from my province has already spoken.
At the present time New Brunswick does not constitute as important a part of this dominion as we did in 1867. At that time, together with the province of Nova Scotia and the province of Canada, as it was called, we were the pillars or the basis of the confederation of Canada. We were therefore quite important then. Today we are not so important. Quite a number of changes in our constitution have taken place since those early days, but most of them have not worked out to the benefit of my province nor to the benefit of the other two maritime provinces, or perhaps I should say the other three maritime provinces as there are today.
In his remarks this afternoon the Prime Minister said-and it has been repeated by some other members-that the people of the dominion knew well that constitutional changes would be brought before this house at this session. I remember that, during the election campaign, the Prime Minister spoke rather casually of this matter in the city of Moncton in my own province. But I want to say that, outside of the Prime Minister himself, I never heard any of the candidates on any side mention constitutional issues during the election campaign. As a matter of fact, the Prime Minister himself tried to impress upon the people of Canada the idea that there

British North America Act were no issues; he said there were no issues in this campaign. The issues which we heard most of during the campaign were the family allowances and the old age pensions. Those were the issues in my own constituency; they were the issues all over my province, as they were in most parts of Canada. Instead of being told that their constitution was to be changed, the people were told that if they did not vote for the Liberal government they were going to lose their baby bonuses and their old age pensions. Those were the chief issues during the campaign, Mr. Speaker.
As I say, I think there is arising in this dominion at the present time an interest over this matter which was not manifested at all during the election campaign. I was rather disappointed at the response of the premier of New Brunswick, Mr. McNair, when he replied to the Prime Minister's letter with regard to the resolution and with regard to the calling together of the various provincial premiers. The Prime Minister's letter was sent out on September 14. The premier of New Brunswick replied to it on September 16. He said:
I am this day in receipt of your letter of September fourteenth which has reference to-
And so on; he mentions this matter of the constitutional changes. My point is this. Instead of giving any consideration to this matter, the premier of New Brunswick simply acknowledged the Prime Minister's letter. He did not even call together his cabinet, as was done by the premiers in most other provinces of the dominion.
Reading the letters, I gather that the only other premier of a province who did not call together his cabinet was the premier of Prince Edward Island, who wrote a three-line letter in acknowledgment of the Prime Minister's. He said that if and when that conference was held, he and his cabinet would be pleased to attend.
The premier of Newfoundland took some time to reply. His letter is dated October 4, and in it he indicates that he had brought the matter fully before his government. Then the premier of Nova Scotia, Hon. Angus L. Macdonald, who has just received some attention from the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis), replied on September 27. He also took the matter up with his colleagues. Despite what the hon. member for Cape Breton South has said this evening, I think that the premier of Nova Scotia reflects the feeling of the people of the three maritime provinces. He said:
There is, I believe, considerable support for the view that the abolition of appeals to the privy council is in effect an amendment of the constitution and that, therefore, it is a question which should be the subject of discussion at the dominion-provincial conference which you suggest.
TMr. Brooks.]
I believe that paragraph expresses the opinion which is quite generally held by the people of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island.
I will not quote further from the letters of the premiers of the various provinces, but the point I wish to make is this. They all took time to consider the letter which was written by the Prime Minister of Canada, except the premier of Prince Edward Island and the premier of New Brunswick. In their replies they also gave considerable attention to the subject matter. But if the premier of our province has not given much attention to this matter, I feel that the people of the province today are giving considerable attention to it. I base my opinion on a report in the Saint John Telegraph-Journal of Monday, October 17. This is an article written by Dr. A. P. Paterson, former New Brunswick minister of education and federal and municipal relations. He was a minister in the Liberal government in the province of New Brunswick. The heading of this article written by Dr. Paterson is as follows:
An Appeal to the People of New Brunswick, in all Walks of Life, to Protect Their Rights and Interest from Misuse of Authority by the Government and Parliament of Canada.
That is a strong heading, Mr. Speaker.

speechtext: He is a man of strong views.

subsubtopic: ADDRESS TO HIS MAJESTY THE KING
speechtext:
As the Prime Minister has said, he is a man of strong views; but he is also a man who has spent most of his life in discussing and studying constitutional matters. I do not know that everybody agrees with him; but then, everyone does not agree with the Prime Minister. Dr. Paterson, however, is a man whose views, I think, are held in quite high esteem by a good many people. In this article Dr. Paterson says:
In the face of Ottawa's speech from the throne, if at any time since New Brunswick was established as a province, we, the people of New Brunswick, needed competent leaders in all walks of life to protect our rights and interests we need them now.
I should like to quote further from Dr. Paterson. In speaking about confederation he had this to say:
The legislatures of the original provinces created the original Dominion of Canada and only the legislature of New Brunswick has the power to agree to amendments of Canada's constitution lawfully so far as this province is concerned. All the authority delegated to the government and parliament of Canada by the provinces, for particular objects, is defined in written documents and Canada's constitution is something sacred not something to be changed or amended by a group of political leaders, except by following the procedure by which it was created.
I would point out, Mr. Speaker, that at the time of confederation the province of New Brunswick was a sovereign state. When

speaking the other day an hon. member said that the provinces were not sovereign states. New Brunswick was never a colony. It was made a province in 1791. In discussing confederation they discussed the problems with Nova Scotia, which was also a sovereign body, and with the province of Canada, which at that time was made up of upper and lower Canada under the Union Act, and afterwards it became the provinces of Ontario and Quebec.
We had such men as Sir Leonard Tilley from New Brunswick, Sir Charles Tupper from Nova Scotia and also Joseph Howe who, as hon. members know, was opposed to confederation. These are some of the very able and outstanding men whom we had in the maritime provinces discussing this matter. I would also point out that in both Nova Scotia and New Brunswick there was a very strong feeling against confederation. These provinces came in not because there was a great feeling in the provinces that we should join with the rest of Canada, but because Sir John A. Macdonald, and other statesmen from what was known as upper Canada at that time, visited the maritime provinces and begged that New Brunswick and Nova Scotia become a part of confederation. I doubt very much whether Canada would ever have become the great country she is today had New Brunswick and Nova Scotia refused to enter confederation at that time. I point out these things, sir, simply to show the importance of our two provinces at the time of the confederation pact.
Since that time New Brunswick and Nova Scotia have lost in importance, but there are two matters that are important to us in these provinces today. One is the matter of taxation, and the other is the matter of representation. So far as representation is concerned, we wish to be assured that we who in the past have lost so many members to the rest of Canada will not lose our representation in the future. That is one of the main points so far as our provinces are concerned. At the time of confederation New Brunswick had a population of around 250,000 people. At that time she was given a representation of fifteen members. Nova Scotia had a population of over 400,000 people. She was given a representation of nineteen members. Today, after all these years, when our population has increased from 250,000 to almost 500,000, instead of fifteen members we have ten. Nova Scotia instead of having nineteen members has thirteen. That is one of the main reasons why we in these little provinces are jealous and afraid of any tampering with the constitution.
Sections 21 and 22 of the British North America Act deal with the composition of the
British North America Act Senate. The representation in the House of Commons is covered by sections 51, 51A and 52 as amended in 1946. Today under these sections the representation of New Brunswick cannot be fewer than the number of senators we have, which is ten. The representation of Prince Edward Island cannot go below four, because that is the number of senators from that province. If, as we sometimes fear, the responsibility of amending our constitution rests entirely with the Dominion of Canada, changes may be made in that representation. Today there are sections in Canada -and I have heard it expressed in the House of Commons-which say that these small provinces down by the sea have been accorded special treatment. They say that we have too much representation. As a matter of fact the late Mr. Woodsworth, who was the leader of the C.C.F. party at one time, said that we were receiving special privileges and it was something which should be corrected. This sentiment exists in Canada. As I have said, I have heard it expressed by hon. members since I have been in the house. For this reason we are exercised over the fact that the provinces of Canada, especially New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island, should not be consulted before any changes are made so far as representation is concerned.
Another important matter is taxation. Today New Brunswick has the largest per capita debt of any province in Canada. We pay the highest taxation of any province in Canada. A few years ago when I happened to be in London I met Sir Andrew Rae Duncan, the man who was responsible for the Duncan report. He asked me what part of Canada I came from. I told him New Brunswick. He said, "You are long-suffering people in the maritime provinces". He told me about making his report for the betterment of conditions in the maritime provinces. He said, "That report has never been implemented. If you depend on the rest of Canada I fear that it never will be implemented". It is on account of the treatment that we have received in the past, not only in the matter of representation, but in the matter of taxation, that we fear this method of amending the British North America Act.
I might also refer to other amendments of the British North America Act. When the territory of Quebec was extended, which was done by an amendment to the British North America Act, we in the maritime provinces received no compensation, although we had helped to pay for the Hudson bay territory which was bought by the dominion government and taken over at that time. The same was true of the boundaries of practically every other province in Canada. Our boundaries were fixed by the British North

British North America Act America Act. The province of Nova Scotia could not expand. New Brunswick could not expand, neither could Prince Edward Island. While we helped to pay, and while I believe these territories belonged in part to these provinces down by the sea, we received no compensation.
We hear hon. members in different parts of the house say that we in the maritime provinces have received special favours as far as representation is concerned. The British North America Act was passed, first, to unite this country into one great dominion; second, to protect minorities; and third, to protect the people who lived in the smaller provinces not only for the time being but for all time. I am emphasizing this because I believe that, unless the provinces are consulted when amendments are made to the British North America Act, they may suffer in the future. These are matters which are not under the jurisdiction of the provinces.
If for instance the representation was under the exclusive jurisdiction of the provinces we would need have no fear; but this is something which is under the jurisdiction of the federal house. The same applies in the matter of financial arrangements which have been made with the different provinces.
Some time ago I spoke on the matter of redistribution, and on that occasion I quoted a statement made by Sir Wilfrid Laurier in 1907 regarding confederation. We have heard it stated continuously in the house that confederation is not a compact. However, we find that in 1907 Sir Wilfrid Laurier said:
Confederation is a compact, made originally by four provinces, but adhered to by all the nine provinces, who have entered it, and I submit to the judgment of this house and to the best consideration of its members, that this compact should not be lightly altered. It should be altered only for adequate cause, and after the provinces themselves have had an opportunity to pass judgment on the same.
Those are the words of a leader of the party of hon. members opposite. He was addressing his remarks to the then hon. member for York, Mr. Crocket, and said:
My hon. friend from York, New Brunswick, stated in the course of his argument that we have announced in the speech from the throne that we are going to ask parliament to alter the financial terms of confederation. That is very true; but my hon. friend should know that we did not come to that conclusion except after conference with the provinces and after all the provincial governments had united in a prayer for the same.
That was a matter of financial arrangement, and Sir Wilfrid Laurier said at that time that they did not come to any agreement until they consulted all the provinces. Surely the arrangements we wish to make regarding the change in our constitution are just as important as was the financial arrangement of 1907.
Sir Robert Borden spoke on the same day. I think all hon. members will agree that he was a great constitutional lawyer. On that Occasion he said:
I agree with what has been said by the right hon. gentleman regarding the undesirability of lightly amending the terms of our constitution and am inclined to agree with him on the necessity of some consultation with the provinces, although of course all the provinces are represented here. But inasmuch as this is a federal compact which we are asked to vary, it is only right that each province should be consulted and its decision given, in the right of its separate entity. But I am not inclined to agree altogether in some of the suggestions urged by my hon. friend.
I have many other quotations here, but I shall not weary the house by quoting them. Most of them have already been placed on Hansard.
Another point has been brought up, namely the suggested inferiority complex of the Canadian people brought about by their having to go to London so often to have our constitution amended. I have seen very little inferiority complex among the people of Canada. We in the maritime provinces fear more the superiority complex of some of our friends from other parts of Canada than we do any inferiority complex which has manifested itself.
Canada is a nation, and has been a nation for many years. I remember reading as a schoolboy some lines of Kipling written over fifty years ago, where he said, in pointing out that Canada was at that time recognized by the British people:
A nation spoke to a nation,
A queen sent word to a throne:
"Daughter am I in my mother's house,
But mistress in my own."
England recognized Canada as a nation in those days; she recognized her as mistress in her own home. I am sure that there was no inferiority complex to be found among the men who took part in the first war. They held their heads high, and felt that as Canadians they were the equal of, indeed if not better than any people with whom they came in contact. The same was true of the men in the second world war. If there was any inferiority complex in Canada, certainly it was not from the men who made Canada the great nation she is. If such a complex has ever existed it may have come from those who possibly did not see the necessity of bearing the burden at that time as did some others.
In closing I would make only two points. The first is that, whatever is done, provision should be made for the protection of the smaller provinces which, I contend, are not in a position either financially or in the matter of population to protect themselves. In my province we always look to the privy council for protection. I have no doubt that
Mr. Brooks-'

the government's intention will be carried out; there is no question in my mind about that. I have no doubt that whatever amendments the government wishes to make it will make. I do appeal to them however to make amendments such as will protect those of us in the smaller provinces. We would prefer to have the provinces consulted, and I feel they should be consulted in all matters pertaining to their future.
I hope, too, that whatever changes are made in the constitution, within the ambit of that constitution there will grow in Canada a stronger nation, and that in future there may be no suggestion of any inferiority complex. We have had none in the past. I believe it is the destiny of this Canada of ours to become the greatest nation in the British commonwealth. I trust that, whatever is done in this parliament, it may be done with that object in view.

Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to speak at great length. I have no quotations from the dead or from big books to offer. Since the beginning of this debate there have been countless quotations from big books or from the speeches of the illustrious dead. These provide interesting reading. However, if we are going to go on like that I suggest we might better adjourn to the library or to the reading room, so that everyone would have an opportunity of becoming a bookworm.
I like better to hear a personal opinion expressed by any one of my colleagues. That is why I enjoyed so much the first portion of the speech by the hon. member for Royal (Mr. Brooks), wherein he voiced the grievances of the maritime provinces. And although I am a great admirer of Sir Wilfrid Laurier and of the other gentleman he quoted, this time I suggest we should consider the proposal before us. I have already congratulated the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) upon his courage in taking this stand to amend the constitution. It is a difficult task. But where would we be if we followed the suggestion made by Mr. Beauchesne before the committee in 1935 and attempted to draft a constitution before a constituent assembly of 225 members? Whoever would think of doing that? We would have something like what happened in France at the time of the assemblee constituante. It would be nothing but chaos and a tower of Babel. It could not be otherwise.
As hon. gentlemen know, the work of the many must be preceded by the work of the few or sometimes by the work of one man. There are those who prepare drafts of legislation or of the work to be handled by a committee so that there may be unity in the subsequent work that is done. There should be
British North America Act direction; there should be a start. First there should be the decision and then something should be offered to the legislative body which is concerned.
Complaints have been made by hon. gentlemen on the other side who are brilliant members of the bar that this matter should be discussed in committee of the whole. That is not necessary because this address will be followed by a bill which will go through all the stages of ordinary legislation-

ADDRESS TO HIS MAJESTY THE KING
speechtext:
The hon. member made one suggestion with respect to holding a session of parliament every year and the term of a parliament, and apparently that was the principal thing that interested him. The question now is not whether amendments will be made at this time; the question is to get permission for this parliament to make amendments later on by means of regular legislation. There would then be an opportunity for all members to ask questions of the government and when that is done I assume that most hon. members will have their minds satisfied by the answers given.

British North America Act
Strong arguments have been put forth by those who contend, on the one hand, that the British North America Act is a compact or contract and those who, on the other hand, contend that it is imperial legislation. It is quite easy to solve that problem; nothing is simpler. In the first place, unquestionably it is an agreement. All we have to do is look at the Quebec resolutions passed in 1864, at the London resolutions adopted at a conference of delegates from the provinces of Canada, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick held at the Westminster Palace hotel, London, December 4, 1866, and at the British North America Act which was assented to on March 29, 1867.
It is clear that the fathers of confederation proceeded by stages. They met first in Charlottetown, adjourned to Quebec, and then to London. While in London they discussed the matter further with the British government. The British North America Act is not composed of the text of the London resolutions, and the London resolutions were not composed of the text of the Quebec resolutions. The British North America Act indicates that there was progress in the discussions, that finally agreement was arrived at and there was a drafting of the act. Not only was there agreement itself; that agreement is wrapped up in an imperial statute. Every time an amendment was made to the constitution the bag was opened.
The main essence of the British North America Act is to be found in the separation of the powers. I have just noted the number of times that the words "exclusive" and "exclusively" are repeated in the two sections which deal with the distribution of powers between parliament and the various legislatures. Section 91 reads:
It shall be lawful for the Queen, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate and House of Commons, to make laws for the peace, order, and good government of Canada, in relation to all matters not coming within the classes of subjects by this act assigned exclusively to the legislatures of the provinces; and for greater certainty, but not so as to restrict the generality of the foregoing terms of this section, it is hereby declared that (notwithstanding anything in this act) the exclusive legislative authority of the parliament of Canada extends to all matters coming within the classes of subjects next hereinafter enumerated, that is to say,-
Then paragraph 29 of that section reads:
Such classes of subjects as are expressly excepte'd in the enumeration of the classes of subjects by this act assigned exclusively to the legislatures of the provinces.
And any matter coming within any of the classes of subjects enumerated in this section shall not be deemed to come within the class of matters of a local or private nature comprised in the enumeration of the classes of subjects by this act assigned exclusively to the legislatures of the provinces.

Now I come to section 92, concerning the exclusive powers of provincial legislatures:
In each province the legislature may exclusively-
"Exclusively" again.
-make laws in relation to matters coming within the classes of subjects next hereinafter enumerated, that is to say...
In section 93 the question of education is dealt with, and in each province the legislature is given exclusive power to make laws concerning this matter. Then we come to section 130, which provides:
Until the parliament of Canada otherwise provides, all officers of the several provinces having duties to discharge in relation to matters other than those coming within the classes of subjects by this act assigned exclusively to the legislatures of the provinces shall be officers of Canada . . .
and so on. It strikes me that the important parts of the act concern the distribution of powers as between Ottawa on the one hand and the provinces on the other. It is abundantly clear that the principle which guided the fathers of confederation in the first place and those who sponsored the act in the second place was to apply to the dominion and the provinces respectively the doctrine "Mind your own business." I believe that is clear. Ottawa was given exclusive jurisdiction to do certain things. On the other hand the provinces were given exclusive jurisdiction to do other things. And so there would be no controversy, no conflict of jurisdiction, it was established in the most definite manner. If in turn the dominion or the provinces have applied to the courts regarding encroachments upon the jurisdiction of the other, it was because in each case someone was complaining that the other party had transgressed the provisions of the act. So the separation of powers was the principal part of our constitution and I do not see how it could be otherwise, unless you wished to change the whole thing from A to Z. But it is an entirely different matter to deal with what concerns only this parliament, without touching what has been left to the exclusive jurisdiction of the provinces.
It is said also that the British North America Act protects the rights of minorities with respect to separate schools and the use of official languages. So there may be no misunderstanding I shall put on record the text of section 133, concerning the use of the English and French languages:
Either the English or the French language may be used by any person in the debates of the houses of the parliament of Canada and of the houses of the legislature of Quebec; and both those languages shall be used in the respective records and journals of those houses; and either of those languages may be used by any person or in any pleading or process in or issuing from any court of Canada established under this act, and in or from all or any of the courts of Quebec.

The acts of the parliament of Canada and of the legislature of Quebec shall be printed and published In both those languages.
That is all we have with respect to the protection of the English and French languages. We can hardly say that is great protection for the French language, and in that respect the constitution has been overrated. With respect to separate schools we have section 93, which hon. members have read and with which they are familiar. That is all.
The Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) spoke of the distribution of powers as between the central government and state or provincial legislative and government bodies; and at page 831 of Hansard he had this to say:
Another consequence of the fact that there Is no procedure Indicated in the British North America Act for its amendment is that there is no prescribed legal protection in that act for the fundamental provisions of our constitution.
Then on page 832:
It is our own responsibility to see that the fundamentals of the Canadian constitution are protected and preserved.
Then, quoting what he had said at Moncton, he went on to say at page 833:
The record of Canadians in two world wars demonstrated beyond any question our ability and our capacity to bear the responsibilities of full nationhood. But our adult nationhood is not yet fully recognized in our constitution and our laws... A method should be worked out to amend our constitution in Canada.
That won't be easy.
That is true.
We do not want the Canadian constitution to be too rigid, but we do want to make sure it contains the fullest safeguards of provincial rights, of the use of the two official languages, and of those other historic rights which are the sacred trusts of our national partnership.
It is our intention after the election to consult the provincial governments with a view to working out a method, which will be satisfactory to all Canadians, of amending the constitution in Canada.
If we are to reaffirm the declaration of the rights of minorities, so much the better. It would be a fine gesture for the parliament of Canada to reaffirm, in a stronger and more decisive manner, what was indicated eighty-two years ago. Here I must tell you, Mr. Speaker, how satisfied I was to listen to all the speeches that have been made, especially the speech by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew). He said something I appreciated greatly, something I have never before heard *rom any leader of his party. At page 837 of Hansard the leader of the opposition said:
There is no suggestion that we must assert our sovereignty, or declare that we are no longer under my limitations. We have asserted that; we have iemonstrated that, and we all believe it.
Well, what is the difference between sov-ireignty and independence? It shows that [DOT]he wind is turning. Progress is being made ;owards Canadian emancipation. On the
British North America Act other hand, we cannot get away from the tradition that has been established in this country. Our ancestors had to fight for their liberty. It was not given to us on a silver platter. Those who contend that it was, ignore and distort history.
At first, our forefathers had great difficulties. They had difficulty in managing their own finances, and they fought for responsible government. I can speak of this because my great-grandfather voted for the ninety-two resolutions that established responsible government in this country. When Baldwin was defeated in York my great-grandfather gave his seat to him. My grandfather voted against confederation. His fear was that it would be a legislative union. My father supported Sir Wilfrid Laurier, who was the leader of the party at the time, and I am satisfied to support the Prime Minister as well as I can in his endeavour to do something that is really a gesture of fine Cana-dianism.
There may be some disagreement. No one expects unanimity at first in the drafting of such an important piece of legislation as the constitution of this country. I am sure that if the Prime Minister, the Leader of the Opposition and the leaders of the other two groups met with the premiers of the provinces, these sons of Canada would do an even better job than was done by the fathers of confederation. It may seem surprising at first, but the only way in which we can arrive at an understanding in the drafting of that part of the constitution which concerns the parliament of Canada is to weed out all the obsolete sections and redraft that act in the same spirit as it was drafted in the first instance.
It is seldom, sir, that the necessary distinction is made between what is ancient and what is antiquated. Some parts of the constitution are antiquated, but it is not because the constitution was drafted and passed eighty-two years ago that it should be changed. I hope that the good spirit that has prevailed in this house since the beginning of the debate will continue until we have a new constitution, which will be accepted not only by this parliament but by all the provinces of Canada. It is my earnest hope because we are now building for the future.
Why should so much importance be given to the opinions of some people who have made a study of this question? Their opinion does not count in this house. They come from outside. They have given some thought to our problems, but why should we quote their books as if the words were gospel. Let the members express their own views. The people of Canada are much more interested in those views than in the views of any

British North America Act author. Let the members support their own opinions by reading the text of the constitution. I am sure all members have done so, but perhaps it would be a good thing to read it again. Then, everyone might realize there is so much good in it that we cannot dispense with it entirely.
For many years, sir, I was concerned about the future of this country. During the war, the policies of all parties and groups were the same with regard to the relations between Canada and Great Britain. In my heart I thought that the destiny of the Liberal party should be to serve Canada first. I expected my party to be a real Canadian party. For many years I waited and suffered in silence, as I said last year. It was only after the present Prime Minister took over the reins of government that we realized the country was advancing in the right direction in matters that have been discussed here with sincerity. I am sure that if the present Prime Minister had not been the leader of the party during the last election, the result would have been different. If he was returned to power with a large majority, it was not due solely to his speech in Moncton about amending the constitution. It was due to the fact that he made speeches in every constituency and appealed to the heart and common sense of the people. A tremendous response was given him because the people realized he was sincere, and was doing his best to promote the welfare and the happiness of our citizens.
I cannot speak much longer, but I sincerely hope that no amendments prejudicial to national unity will be sponsored by this government. I am sure that will not be the case. I shall ask my colleagues, and I shall urge upon them, the necessity of showing the same spirit in this house as should prevail at a meeting of those who would be called to draft a new constitution. The speeches that have been made during the course of this debate are a credit to each member. I make no exceptions. Whether the members spoke from this side or the other side of the house, they have done their best. Sometimes they have used hasty words, but that is of no consequence. The tenor of the debate has been good. I congratulate all my colleagues on what they have done; I congratulate the government. I again wish them success. I hope that there will be amicable discussion with the provinces of all phases of the act. I also hope that the provinces will show the same spirit as Ottawa has shown. There is no question of encroaching upon the rights of anyone. If the thing is done by the legislation that would follow the permission to amend the constitution, they will all be there to see to it and to defend the traditions of the past.


But I will tell my friend the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis), whom I admire, and who has the natural gift of eloquence and persuasion, that he should come to the province of Quebec. It is a bit late now, but next summer if he wishes to come to my constituency I will drive him around and will give him the opportunity of meeting the people of my province. Then I am sure that he will change his views.

May I ask the hon. gentleman this question: Where do we go from here if this resolution passes?
(Translation):

subsubtopic: ADDRESS TO HIS MAJESTY THE KING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on June 19, 1946, during the debate on redistribution, I stated, in this house, that the British North America Act was a compact which could not be amended without the consent of the parties thereto.
The resolution before us gives me the opportunity of coming back briefly to this argument and of pointing out once again that the consent of the provinces is needed to amend the Canadian constitution. The late Minister of Justice, the Right Hon. Ernest Lapointe, whose name has been repeatedly mentioned in the debate, stated in this house in 1925 that confederation was based on a compact between the provinces who reached a compromise and granted certain rights to the federal authority, but the central power may not alter the constitution without first securing the permission of the provinces, which are responsible for it and work with the federal authority under a well-balanced division of powers and responsibilities. Sir Robert Borden, during the course of a debate, also stated:
There is no need of changing the terms of our constitution and I am inclined to believe that it would be necessary to consult the provinces.
It is also the opinion of Mr. Arthur B. Keith, an authority on constitutional law. In his book "Responsible Government in the Dominions" he states that it was explicitly recognized by the imperial government in 1907 that confederation is a pact which cannot be altered without first obtaining the consent of the provinces. Lord Carnarvon and Viscount Haldane, both eminent jurists, were always of that opinion. The same applies to the fathers of confederation, Sir John Macdonald, George Brown and Thomas D'Arcy McGee, who said:
The document on the clerk's table Is a contract.

I now come to Lord Sankey who stated: (Text):
The process of interpretation as the years go on ought not to be allowed to dim or to whittle down the provision of the original contract upon which confederation is founded.
In 1938, in the minimum wage case Lord Atkin, in delivering the decision of the privy council, speaks of the distribution of powers between the dominion and the provinces under the act as "the interprovincial compact".
The attitude of Downing street may be found in a dispatch of March 18, 1865, to the Hon. Arthur Hamilton Gordon, Lieutenant Governor of New Brunswick. The cordial approval of the proceedings of the Quebec conference is here given.
Measures based on the plan drawn up by the delegates at the Quebec conference would be submitted to the imperial parliament if the provincial legislatures should sanction that plan.
It is evident from this undertaking that the right was conceded to the provinces to conclude an agreement which was in the nature of a treaty among themselves.
(Translation):
In pretending that the B.N.A. Act is only a statute, the Prime Minister sets aside the aside the unequivocal opinions and expressed views of statesmen and jurists such as Alexander Campbell, Langevin, Cartier, Galt, Tache, Adderley, Laurier, Mercier, Meighen, Ferguson, Bennett, Borden, Mignault, Loran-ger, and others. He asserts that we have been wrong for eighty years and that we must henceforth abide by his point of view with respect to the act of 1867. And yet, since the time of confederation, all our leaders, without exception, have recognized that it is impossible to amend the B.N.A. Act without consulting the provinces.
Mr. Speaker, I am convinced that never would the French Canadians have agreed, in 1867, to the passing of a law liable to interpretation and amendment according to the wishes of only one of the contracting parties. If it had been the intention of the fathers of confederation to wrong us, to deceive us and to leave us at the mercy of an encroaching central power, they would simply have deprived us by stealth of our rights and prerogatives, taking away from us the freedom to live as we thought fit, to be our own masters. In that case, we would not be bound to observe the provisions of this act. Lower Canada did not want a legislative union and we do not want it any more today.
Mr. Speaker, no province is as highly concerned as the province of Quebec with the procedure to be followed in amending our constitution.
British North America Act
Because of our mentality, our traditions, our language and our faith, this is a vital matter. Let us not forget that in 1867, at the time of confederation, the province of Quebec negotiated on an equal footing with the other provinces and represented, above all else, a national entity. Nowadays, people scoff at our claims. Yet, the hundreds of millions of dollars which, every year, we pour into the dominion treasury should give us a voice in the affairs of the country.
Confederation was more than a pact between nations; it was also a pact between two great races. No one can amend the British North America Act without consulting the province of Quebec, cradle of the Frenchspeaking community in Canada. The Canadian state owes its existence to the provinces that brought it into being. These same provinces also continue to provide it with the funds it needs to survive.
If the British North America Act does not afford sufficient protection for the rights of the provinces, what assurance have we that future amendments will guarantee us more? Under the pretext of rendering our constitution more pliable, they are endangering rights and prerogatives that are much more important than such pliability itself.
The constitution is above the federal government; it cannot be amended by that government alone since it is the result of a compact between New Brunswick and Nova Scotia, as well as Upper and Lower Canada- that is Ontario and Quebec-to which were subsequently added our other provinces. We are told about this procedure not having been followed in the past, and about the number of times the constitution was amended without prior consultation of the provinces. We are now asked to add a new precedent to those already established. We do not wish to be tied down by what has already been done; we refuse to be the accomplices of previous violations. If we did not act properly several times, are we justified in doing it over again? Repeated illegalities have never produced anything legal. There is no clause in the British North America Act indicating the way in which it can be amended. Was that omission not deliberate?
The province of Quebec is now being attacked because it has no faith in the gospel of centralization. Yet we know very well that Messrs. Mercier, Gouin and Taschereau, former liberal prime ministers of my province, were violently opposed to centralization and highly in favour of provincial autonomy. The men are no more, but the doctrines and principles remain unchanged.
In establishing the supreme court, whose judges are appointed by the governor in
994

British North America Act council, as the final tribunal on constitutional disputes, this parliament, which determines the powers and duties of those judges, thereby indicates that henceforth our constitution will be amended at the discretion of the party in power. So much the worse if a mistake is made. In fact it is not easy, as was seen in the past, to determine what matters come under the central power's jurisdiction and what matters are within the purview of the provinces.
(Text):
Writing in the Toronto Saturday Night on September 27, Mr. B. K. Sandwell said:
Many of the provincall fields have extremely vague boundaries and these boundaries could be contracted without the slightest trouble by an amendment merely asserting a hitherto uncertified power of the dominion. Civil rights, as a provincial field, could be reduced to the area which it occupied in the 'seventies, before the provincializing tendency began, by merely enacting that the dominion has power to do things which it actually did in that period but which later judicial decisions prevent it from doing except under the emergency doctrine. A sympathetic supreme court would declare that this amendment relates "to matters not coming", et cetera, and there you are; the thing is done.
The provinces will certainly maintain that they have rights, or at any rate vested interest, extending far beyond the limits of section 92. The definition of the powers to be vested in parliament would certainly, for example, enable it to reduce the number of members sent to Ottawa by Prince Edward Island, which is specially provided for by the constitution but has nothing whatever to do with the jurisdiction of the provincial legislature.
(Translation):
We are exhorted to have respect for and confidence in our judicial system; we hear a lot-and rightly so-about the integrity of those who hold the foremost place in that system. Fine, I am all for it. However if we want that system to remain what it is, if we want justice to be above politics, we should not confront judges with the alternative of having to displease the party who chose them or the members who set the limit of their sovereignty.
Being free of the necessity of going to Westminster to amend our constitution is one more step towards our final emancipation. I am highly pleased about it but that liberating step should not be taken at the expense of the sacred agreements which were signed in 1867. The adoption of the procedure suggested by the government would place before the provinces a fait accompli. We would bring them into subjection, deprive them of their autonomy to make that of Canada more secure. Might has never made right, and I do not think that the procedure resorted to today by the federal government is likely to promote harmony and good understanding between the different parts of this dominion. Certain provinces want to be con-


suited; well, let them be consulted! Good manners would at least require that they be informed as to the way in which it is intended to proceed to destroy the last trace of their autonomy.
The extreme haste displayed by the government authorities in the settlement of this all-important matter is surprising and disturbing to those who are concerned with Canada's future.
We are assured that not one minority right is endangered at present, but who knows what tomorrow has in store? The effects of this measure will be felt much later. The future generations may deplore our having thus upset the constitution of 1867 which, although it was not always very efficient in preventing encroachments by the central power, has at least restrained efforts of centralizers. If dominion governments had always respected the spirit of the constitution, if part of the population had not been brought, through propaganda and election speeches, to believe that the time had come to modernize the British North America Act, that the latter no longer met the needs of the Ottawa politicians; if instead of a constant effort toward centralization, an endeavour had been made to bring about a decentralization of powers and administration we would not witness the jurisdiction conflicts which confront us today.
The refusal on the part of the Prime Minister to consult the provinces before taking action is more than regrettable, and I desire to register my protest in this regard.

subsubtopic: ADDRESS TO HIS MAJESTY THE KING
speechtext:
Since it is so late in the evening and since we have had so much fine debating I hesitate to rise to take part in the debate. My only reason for doing so is to show how the question before us appears to an ordinary Canadian like myself unlearned in the art of analysing constitutions.
Before I start to develop the points I wish to make I want to make it abundantly clear that I am personally supporting the resolution that is now before us. I am supporting it because, first, I do not believe that it interferes in any way with the rights of the provinces; second, I believe that it would be a mistake for this government to approach the provinces before it has gone as far as it is possible to go without that consultation. I believe that it would weaken the position of this government and be a disservice to the country to do that.
I think we have made progress. We all agree on at least one point, namely, that we should take to ourselves here in Canada the full power to amend our constitution. So far I have not heard any difference of opinion on that point. Our disagreement arises when

'we begin to consider how we are to take to ourselves that power. I will agree at once that there are legitimate grounds for differences. The government proposes to make the change in two steps, the first of which is proposed in this resolution, whereby we should petition the parliament at Westminster to amend the British North America Act where matters concerning federal jurisdiction only are concerned.
The question has been raised as to who shall define the field as between federal and provincial jurisdiction. It seems to me that that is not a difficult question to answer. If this resolution carries, and if the British parliament makes the change asked for, the line between federal and provincial jurisdiction will be defined as it has always been defined, namely, by the courts of the country.
After this resolution is passed and the amendment is made, if the federal parliament encroaches upon the field of provincial jurisdiction, I am quite sure the courts will declare such action ultra vires, just as it would have been ultra vires before the passing of this resolution. I do not believe, therefore, that there is any great difficulty in that respect.
This party agrees with the government's method of amendment. As I have already said, we believe it would be bad policy to approach the provincial governments seeking agreement with them on this first step. It might not be possible to come to agreement, and I doubt if we would be then in as good a position to proceed with this resolution as we are today. The official opposition and the Social Credit party disagree with this method, and, as I said before, there are legitimate grounds for disagreement. In my opinion, however, the argument is now all in favour of the government's method. Like the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot), I am not greatly impressed by quotations from the speeches and opinions of the great men of the past. I must admit however that I was rather surprised to hear the hon. member for Temiscouata make that statement, because of his profession-a profession in which nearly all opinions are based upon some hoary and musty precedents of ancient times.

Macdonald or Sir Wilfrid Laurier. I think, too, that we have today men who are just as great as were those men, great as they appear to have been. Perhaps they only seem 45781-631
British North America Act great to us, because we know them only by tradition. I should not like to detract anything from that tradition which has grown with the years. While a person sitting as I do on the opposition side of the house should always be careful not to give comfort to the enemy, I am of the opinion that the present Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), when history is written, as the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) would say, will stand up with the best of them.

speechtext:
Well, you can't say I didn't make a good try.
Those were placid and simple times in comparison with the swift-moving conditions which the statesmen of today have to meet. And here may I point out that it is world economic conditions, and how those conditions affect Canada, that cause us to give so much attention to changing our constitution. Changes have become necessary to meet the needs of today, which have changed so much since 1867.
It is really only since the thirties that there has been any great demand in this country for constitutional changes. The need for change began to become apparent around that time, because under the British North America Act the provinces were charged with responsibilities they did not have the resources to discharge. And we will soon reach the same condition again, when the post-war period of prosperity is over, where the provinces will not be able to discharge the responsibilities given them under the constitution. When that day comes the provinces themselves in conjunction with the federal government will initiate and work out the changes that will be necessary to enable them to discharge the responsibilities with which they are confronted.
This afternoon the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) referred to an amendment moved to a resolution in the house in 1925 by the former leader of this party, the late Mr. Woodsworth. He pointed out that Mr. Woodsworth wanted changes made only with the consent of the provinces. Like other men-and I think like all other men whose opinions are worth anything-Mr. Woodsworth held his views only so long as they were supported by facts. If the facts no longer support them, it would be a foolish man indeed who continued to hold the same opinion.
I find that in volume I of Hansard for 1935

British North America Act Mr. Woodsworth introduced a resolution, to which reference has already been made, asking the house to set up a special committee to study and report on the best method by which the British North America Act might be amended. In support of that resolution he said, as reported on page 219 of Hansard:
Further I think it is fairly generally conceded that the consent of the provinces is not necessary, at least from the legal standpoint. There was a time when we were told that we could not amend the British North America Act without the consent of all the provinces, that in fact confederation was something in the nature of a treaty and that it could not be changed without the consent of all parties. I think that theory has been absolutely discarded, and we need not continue to debate it.
Then on page 218 of the same Hansard appears a report of what the late Mr. Lapointe said on May 11, 1931, which reads as follows:
Again I say that to insist on having the consent of all the provinces to every change would be asking almost an impossibility; to ask that either British Columbia in the west or Prince Edward Island in the east should be able to block a change with which it is essential for the federal power to go ahead within the limits of its jurisdiction on certain matters, I do not think would be right; but on essential matters, such matters, for instance, as the protection of minorities, of language, of schools, as they are inserted in the British North America Act, I believe it should not be possible to make a change without the consent of all.
The matters mentioned by Mr. Lapointe, which were not to be interfered with are the same as in the resolution now before us. I think that his is the only position anyone can take. The hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) made what I thought was an unfavourable comparison between the constitutions of Canada and the United States. He mentioned that there was no charter of liberty or declaration of the rights of man in the Canadian constitution. I think if history has demonstrated anything it is that paper constitutions are very poor things on which to lean. I think history has amply proved that if freedom, liberty, toleration and justice are not written into the traditions, habits, hearts and souls of a people, there is little protection in a written constitution, as so many people in the United States and elsewhere know at the present time and have known for many, many years. I think I can give this house a good example of the value of written constitutions by quoting from "Men and Politics" by Louis Fischer. I think most hon. members have read this book as it was a "best-seller" a few years ago. Referring to the Soviet union he says this at page 335:
The constitution, now the supreme law of the Soviet union, does two things; It describes a system of government and it enunciates a bill of rights. The bill of rights is inspiring. But there is nothing in the system of government to safeguard the rights. The popular enjoyment of the rights thus depends


on the good will of the person or persons who control the government, and they have chosen to ignore the right. One of the latest violations of the bill of rights is the introduction of payment for tuition in high schools and colleges. This contravenes article 121 of the constitution which says:
"Citizens of the Soviet union have a right to education. The right is implemented by universal, compulsory, elementary education and by free education, including university education."
The government did not ask the people or parliament whether it could introduce paid education. The constitution was not amended to allow paid education. The government simply decreed paid tuition by ukase and that was all there was to it except for the pain in the hearts of many silent people.
I do not say that, in a country such as Canada where government by majority has been accepted for so long a time, where it has become a tradition in the minds and hearts of the people, safeguards in our constitution are not a good thing. That is why 1 support the resolution with the safeguards that were originally in it as well as those which have been added by the amendment moved by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) and the amendment to that amendment moved by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson).
On motion of Mr. Maclnnis the debate was adjourned.
